title: How to Build an AI Code Review Agent - Daksh Gupta, Greptile
talk_summary: Greptile's co-founder explains how to build an AI code review agent: sandbox + agent + PR webhook is the easy part, but naive versions miss bugs, lack codebase context, cost $3-25/PR, produce nitpicks, and find 'new' bugs on every rerun. He prescribes prompt tuning around a catalog of your own bug types, a historical PR regression dataset, model inversion (review with a different model family than wrote the code), a codebase knowledge base/wiki instead of grep, autonomous vision-based E2E testing, and routing ~20% of subtasks to frontier models with cheap models for the long tail.

takeaways.what_they_do: Review code with a different model family than the one that generated it, because same-family models fail the same way in review as in generation; detect the generating agent via branch names/co-author trailers, heuristics for the rest.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you're using the same model to review the code written by the same model... you'll actually have relatively fewer bugs caught
takeaways.numbers: 10% higher catch rate when flipping models

takeaways.technique: Bug-type catalog + explicit nitpick suppression in review prompt
takeaways.what_they_do: Mine past outages/incidents for the bug classes your codebase actually produces, put that catalog in the review prompt as the things to look for, and explicitly define what counts as a nitpick and forbid it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Create a catalog of them, and then have your prompt look for those specific bug types.

takeaways.technique: Historical-PR regression set for the reviewer
takeaways.what_they_do: Build a dataset of past PRs that caused incidents and re-run every reviewer version against it to measure catch frequency, because you cannot observe the absence of bugs in production.
takeaways.evidence_quote: have any version of your review agent run through those and see with what frequency it can catch those bugs
takeaways.numbers: ~1 in 1000 PRs (or lines) has a catastrophic bug

takeaways.what_they_do: Split review into ~20 subtasks and assign each a specific model: cheap models for context-finding, file reads, and computer-use; frontier models only for bug analysis and final review submission.
takeaways.evidence_quote: our share today is about 20% frontier models for the most critical tasks
takeaways.numbers: 20% frontier / 80% cheap; 20 subtasks; claims 70-80% of the benefit from simple swaps

takeaways.technique: Codebase knowledge base instead of raw grep
takeaways.what_they_do: Index the whole codebase into a wiki/knowledge base (auth flows, diagrams, files involved per subsystem) and use a cheap model to re-rank which context pieces to load, so the agent never reads files it doesn't need.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we produce an internal knowledge base where we essentially check across the entire code base all the different parts, catalog them, and then index

takeaways.technique: Vision-based autonomous E2E in dependency-rich sandbox
takeaways.what_they_do: Spin the real stack up in a configurable VM per PR branch, document app flows, and have an agent drive the UI with computer-use/vision models to catch things static review can't (e.g. button hidden on iPhone).
takeaways.evidence_quote: Reptile's agent uses computer vision to test them end to end
